newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam moves to bolster economy, faith in banks.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam moves to bolster economy, faith in banks.

text.p: Vietnam slashed interest rates on Monday to tackle flagging economic growth and rounded on reports questioning the ability of the troubled banking system to meet financial commitments.

In a rare news conference for both local and foreign reporters, the central bank denied that the authorities had instructed commercial banks to withhold payments to foreign banks on letter of credit guarantees.

State Bank of Vietnam Deputy Governor Le Duc Thuy said commercial banks, including state-owned Vietcombank, had missed payments on some letters of credit -- but insisted that this was due to internal regulatory problems rather than policy.

"The government and the State Bank have requested Vietnamese commercial banks and enterprises to honour their commitments to their partners in accordance with international law and practices," Thuy said.

The conference came in response to the international financial community's growing concern about repeated bank defaults on short-term trade financing and the central bank's wherewithal to act as a lender of last resort.

Thomson BankWatch, a New York-based credit rating agency, last week cut its Vietnamese sovereign risk rating and also its short-term local currency rating for nine prominent banks, in their case to sub-investment grade.
Doubts about the country's creditworthiness could not have come at a more awkward time.
Hanoi is hoping tie up a Brady-style bond deal to restructure its foreign commercial bank debt by the end of August and is hoping to make a debut eurobond issue sometime after that.
The country is also heavily dependent on financing from abroad and could not afford to see foreign credit lines reeled in, especially at a time when the economy is coming off the boil.
The central bank, pointing to a slide in inflation and slower industrial output and credit, said it had lowered the ceiling on interest rates with effect from Tuesday.

It said the limit on short-term local currency loans would be reduced by 0.25 percentage point to 1.00 percent a month, while the cap on medium- and long-term lending would also be 0.25 percentage point lower at 1.10 percent.

The limits were last cut in October after inflation fell to an annual 2.9 percent, its lowest since economic reform was launched in the late 1980s. But the deflationary climate has persisted since then, with inflation at just 2.1 percent this month.
Thuy said the value of letters of credit at the end of March was $1.3 billion. Asked how much of such financing Vietnamese banks had failed to repay by the due date, he said six percent.

A senior Vietcombank official told Reuters last week that internal regulations prevented banks from dipping into their own funds if a client failed to pay or from forcing a cash-strapped client to take out a new loan.

Adherence to that rule has alarmed foreign banks, which say international regulations -- requiring banks to honour debt guarantees regardless of whether they get paid themselves -- must take precedence where foreign parties are involved.
Thuy said efforts were under way to improve the regulatory framework, but stressed that when it has foreign commitments Vietnam would abide by international practices.
